rationale:
Today has no Lane C news. TRANSCEND-T2D-2 is about 72 h old, it already had a Lane C long-form on 10-29, and its 10-29 dysesthesia Short used up this week's one Short for that trial. So the long-form goes to Lane A, following the playbook queue. Stopping (10-27), plateau (10-27), bones and muscle (10-28), protein (10-29) and hair loss (10-30) are all done, so the next topic is food noise and cravings. It has strong search demand and sits next to What to Eat and Side Effects, which helps suggested traffic. The body rests on settled, peer-reviewed evidence about how GLP-1 acts on the brain's appetite and reward systems, plus published human appetite and craving studies. The Oct 29 grocery-purchase paper is only the intro hook.

Shorts:
- **08:00 body worry: fatigue.** This is a new topic, and the Zepbound label gives clean figures by dose against placebo.
- **13:00 lead: the thyroid boxed warning, as a calm "what's confirmed?" Short.** It explains detection bias. None of the playbook's 13:00 options qualifies today: there's no new head-to-head, the retatrutide trial has used its one Short this week, and there's no fresh dated gray-market fact. The thyroid piece also covers the myth-busting share of the mix.
- **20:00 funnel Short (Exp D): spin-off of L1.** It asks one fresh question, what the new grocery-purchase study measured, so it doesn't repeat the 10-06 or 10-29 food-noise Shorts.

The pieces cover different body systems: brain and appetite, energy, and thyroid. Every piece carries "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line, with no dosing, switching or sourcing talk. The quota calls for no carousels, which matches the analytics, so none are planned.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and food noise: what GLP-1 and GIP signalling does in the brain's appetite and reward areas, what human studies of appetite and cravings show, what the new grocery-purchase study measured, and habits that help when food noise comes back
pieces.angle: Keep everything except chapter 4. Replace 'the new grocery-purchase study (DOM, Oct 29, 2026)' with: 'What happens to what people buy? A Danish study of supermarket receipts (JAMA Network Open, 2026)'. Give 293 GLP-1 starters versus 884 matched non-users, and call it observational purchase data, not what people actually ate. Say the changes were 'modest' and 'linked to' starting the drug. Say which GLP-1 medicines it covered only as the paper reports them, and don't say tirzepatide unless the paper does. Use the DOM Oct 29 paper only if a human or the scriptwriter opens its abstract and confirms the drugs, population, design and findings. Otherwise drop it. Main human anchor: Heise 2023 Diabetes Care (type 2 diabetes, tirzepatide vs semaglutide vs placebo, appetite and energy intake at a test lunch). Label every brain-reward finding by species. Chapter 5: SURMOUNT-4 shows weight regain after switching to placebo, not food noise directly. Say 'many people report hunger coming back' only as an unsourced, plainly hedged observation, or leave it out.

pieces.why: Next topic in the Lane A queue. Lane A is the engine (median about 232 min, about 6.6× other GLP-1 long-forms), and this one sits next to What to Eat and Side Effects for suggested traffic. The body rests on settled mechanism and trial evidence. | fact-check: The Lane A topic, safety framing, chapter plan and title are sound. The title is 45 characters and its first sentence answers it. Mechanism plus human-study chapters can be fully sourced. One problem: I could not confirm that the 'new grocery-purchase study (Diabetes Obes Metab, Oct 29, 2026)' exists. Several extended searches found only one supermarket-receipt study. It is Danish and appeared in JAMA Network Open in early 2026: 'Consumer Food Purchases After Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist Initiation', from the SMIL cohort at Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen. It followed 1,177 adults: 293 who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist and 884 matched non-users. It found modest drops in calories, sugar, carbohydrate and saturated fat per 100 g of food bought, a slight rise in protein and a shift toward less ultra-processed food. I also saw a DOM record (dom.71408) but couldn't open it (403), so I can't say what it reports. Verified human appetite anchor for tirzepatide: Heise et al., Diabetes Care 2023;46(5):998–1004. This randomized, double-blind trial in people with type 2 diabetes compared tirzepatide with semaglutide and placebo. Both drugs reduced appetite compared with placebo, and tirzepatide reduced energy intake at an all-you-can-eat lunch. Say 'people with type 2 diabetes' and don't give dose numbers on screen or in the narration. Label any semaglutide-only data as semaglutide. Most reward-system evidence ('wanting' vs 'liking') comes from rodents, so label it 'in mice/rats'. Don't claim tirzepatide's GIP part acts in the human brain; that's unproven in people. 'Food noise' is a lay term, not a diagnosis; keep it that way. Stopping chapter: SURMOUNT-4 measured weight regain, not food noise. Don't say it showed food noise returning; say only that weight was regained on placebo (+14.0% from week 36 to week 88), plus the don't-stop line.

pieces.topic: Does tirzepatide make you tired? Fatigue in the Zepbound label (5%, 6% and 7% by dose vs 3% on placebo, pooled SURMOUNT-1 and -2) and common, checkable reasons
pieces.angle: 08:00 calm 'honest uncertainty' body-worry Short, 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer. Open within 10 s: 'Feeling wiped out on tirzepatide? Fatigue is on the label, but it's uncommon: 5 to 7 percent across doses versus 3 percent on placebo in the trials.' Verify the figures and the pooled-trial population against the FDA label itself, not Healthline. One line: eating much less, low fluids or skipped protein can all leave you tired. That's 'can', not proven cause. Then what's worth checking with a clinician: how much you're eating and drinking, and whether blood tests make sense (iron and others). No supplement promises and no dosing. Red flag: dizziness or fainting, or vomiting with signs of dehydration, means contact your prescriber promptly. One GI line. 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. Loop ending, no emoji, mix at 0.02 or lower.

pieces.why: A new body-worry question with clean label numbers. Body-worry Shorts with tirzepatide in the title are proven (median about 103), and Instagram favours calm life-on-drug topics.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and the thyroid warning: what's confirmed? The boxed warning comes from rodent C-cell tumours; human data are reassuring but limited; more thyroid scans can mean more cancers found (Diabetes Res Clin Pract scoping review, Oct 27, 2026)
pieces.angle: Facts 1 and 2 in exact label wording (rats; unknown in humans; contraindicated with personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2). Fact 3: 'In one large observational study of adults with type 2 diabetes, thyroid cancer diagnoses rose only in the first year after starting a GLP-1 medicine, when people also had more thyroid scans. The authors say that points to finding existing cancers sooner (detection bias), not new ones caused by the drug. It wasn't tirzepatide-specific, and rare cancers like MTC are hard to study.' Cite the JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg study (PubMed record) rather than the unverified Oct 27 DRCP review, unless that review's abstract is confirmed. Keep the label symptom list, the 'tell your healthcare provider' line, the don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line. Title can stay.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Thyroid Warning: What's Actually Confirmed? #shorts
pieces.why: A top evergreen fear search with a fresh peer-reviewed hook. The detection-bias explanation is a contrarian-but-true, myth-busting angle that few channels cover. | fact-check: Facts 1 and 2 match the Zepbound boxed warning on DailyMed exactly. Quoted: 'In rats, tirzepatide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell tumors at clinically relevant exposures. It is unknown whether ZEPBOUND causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans…' It is contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2. Problem: I could not find the 'Diabetes Res Clin Pract scoping review, Oct 27, 2026' in several extended searches. Don't build Fact 3 on it unless its abstract is opened and confirmed. A verified detection-bias source exists: a JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery observational study (Mayo Clinic) of 351,913 adults with type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 RA starters had more thyroid cancer diagnoses only in the first year, along with more thyroid ultrasounds, which suggests detection bias. Caveats: it covers GLP-1 RAs as a class in type 2 diabetes, it's observational, and it isn't tirzepatide-specific. Also, MTC is rare, so studies have limited power to detect it. Say 'human studies so far haven't shown a clear increase, but the data are limited', never 'safe' or 'no risk'.

pieces.topic: What happens to your grocery cart on a GLP-1 medicine? The digital food-purchase study before and after GLP-1-based treatment (Diabetes Obes Metab, Oct 29, 2026)
pieces.angle: If the DOM Oct 29 abstract can't be opened and confirmed, base the Short on the JAMA Network Open 2026 Danish receipt study. Opening line: 'After starting a GLP-1 medicine, people in a Danish study bought groceries with slightly fewer calories and less sugar per 100 grams, and a little more protein.' Then: observational; 293 starters versus 884 matched non-users; purchase receipts, not what people ate; 'linked to', not proof; the changes were modest. Title must name only the drugs the paper covered. If it reports only 'GLP-1 receptor agonists', use e.g. 'GLP-1 Medicines and Your Grocery Cart: What Changed #shorts'. Accuracy wins over the tirzepatide-first title rule here. Drop 'new' from the title. Keep the one biology line from L1's verified wording, the GI line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line, and the closing funnel line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Your Grocery Cart: What a New Study Found #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It's today's 20:00 Exp D funnel Short, driving viewers to the food noise long-form with a new, dated peer-reviewed fact. | fact-check: Same issue as L1: the 'Diabetes Obes Metab, Oct 29, 2026' digital food-purchase study couldn't be confirmed. The receipt study I could confirm is the Danish SMIL study in JAMA Network Open (early 2026): 293 GLP-1 RA starters versus 884 matched non-users, purchases logged through an app. That data is about nine months old, so don't call it 'new'. The title is risky: there's no evidence the Danish study covered tirzepatide users. Its period and setting suggest mostly semaglutide or other GLP-1 RAs. The brief's own rule says to put tirzepatide in the title only if the paper covered it. The changes were small, so the Short must say 'modest' and 'per 100 g of food bought'. It shouldn't imply people ate healthier or lost weight because of what they bought. Don't label foods 'bad'. Neutral wording like 'less ultra-processed' is fine if it's the paper's term.
